CBF-Based Control Allocation for
Omnidirectional Tiltrotor Aerial Robots

Seobeom Lee    Hyondong Oh ††thanks: Seobeom Lee and Hyondong Oh are with the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Daejeon, Republic of Korea (e-mail: seobeomlee@kaist.ac.kr; h.oh@kaist.ac.kr).††thanks: Corresponding author: Hyondong Oh (e-mail: h.oh@kaist.ac.kr).
Abstract

Actively tilting aerial robots can generate six-dimensional wrenches, but slow servo response can make a desired wrench infeasible during reconfiguration. This paper develops a control barrier function (CBF) allocator that preserves wrench feasibility under bounded servo-configuration mismatch. An exact equivalent-wrench identity connects the thrust required at nominal and actual configurations. For a nonsingular six-channel allocation map, inverse allocation reduces robust wrench containment to twelve thrust margins tightened by an ellipsoidal reserve. Their complete derivatives yield a six-variable servo-rate quadratic program, followed by differential thrust allocation for tracking. A conditional forward-invariance result establishes actual-configuration feasibility under reserve coverage, feasible initialization, and admissible CBF inputs. A complementary MuJoCo study evaluates a measured-angle implementation against geometric, augmented differential, and normalized differential allocation in circular and cartwheel maneuvers, with and without disturbances. The proposed implementation achieves lower position error in all four recorded scenarios, with an attitude tradeoff in circular tracking. During the disturbed cartwheel, the desired wrench is feasible at all 1751 stored samples of continuous rotation; baseline violation rates range from 60.8% to 100%. These comparisons evaluate sampled feasibility; validation of the nominal-trajectory certificate requires nominal-state and reserve-coverage records.

Index Terms: 
Aerial systems, control allocation, control barrier functions, omnidirectional robots, actuator constraints.

I Introduction

Omnidirectional aerial robots can regulate position and attitude independently, enabling contact inspection, tool alignment, and six-dimensional physical interaction [1, 2, 3]. Fixed tilted-rotor designs obtain this capability through their geometry [4, 5], whereas actively tilting platforms can reorient their thrust directions during flight [6, 7]. In the latter case, control allocation must coordinate fast thrust changes with slower servo motion.

Servo transients can make a desired wrench infeasible even when the target pose is kinematically admissible. A force and moment achievable after reorientation may lie outside the thrust-limited set at the current tilt angles. Aggressive motion therefore requires an allocator that preserves wrench authority while both the request and the actuation geometry evolve.

Wrench tracking and instantaneous feasibility are distinct objectives. Tracking reduces the difference between the desired and generated wrench; feasibility requires an admissible thrust vector at the current rotor directions. Servo motion changes the attainable wrench set. We constrain that motion to retain the requested wrench together with a neighborhood accounting for nominal-to-actual configuration mismatch.

Geometric and differential allocators provide direct actuator setpoints, coordinated reconfiguration, and limit handling [8, 7, 9]. Augmented and normalized differential allocation further connect wrench controllers to actuator-rate commands and account for heterogeneous limits [10]. The remaining question addressed here is how to constrain servo reconfiguration so that a specified wrench request remains inside the instantaneous thrust-limited set despite configuration mismatch.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) express this objective as constraints on servo motion [11, 12]. For a nonsingular six-channel configuration, inverse allocation gives six lower and six upper thrust margins. An ellipsoidal wrench reserve tightens them against nominal-to-actual configuration mismatch. Their complete derivatives, including the changing reserve, define a servo-rate quadratic program (QP); a downstream differential allocator commands thrust rates for tracking.

The contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    An exact nominal-to-actual required-thrust identity and a support-based reduction of configuration-robust wrench containment to twelve scalar margins.

  2. 2.

    An explicit servo-rate CBF-QP and a conditional invariance proof connecting nominal margins to desired-wrench feasibility at the actual servo angles, without assuming identical commanded and actual servo velocities.

  3. 3.

    A telemetry-based comparison of a measured-angle CBF variant with geometric allocation (GA), augmented differential allocation (ADA), and normalized differential allocation (NDA) across four scenarios. Recorded force-space views and six-dimensional margins relate tracking performance to instantaneous wrench feasibility.

The guarantee concerns existence of an admissible thrust vector; thrust realization and pose tracking also depend on actuator and closed-loop dynamics.

Sections III–IV establish the model and baseline allocators. Sections V–VI develop the CBF formulation and guarantee. Sections VII–IX present the simulation comparison, design implications, and conclusions.

II Related Work

II-A Actuation Geometry and Dynamic Allocation

The attainable wrench set depends on both vehicle design and rotor orientation. Offline tilt optimization improves task-dependent authority [13], synchronized mechanisms change the flight configuration [14], and independently tilting platforms permit online redistribution of actuator effort [6, 7]. These architectures offer different allocation freedoms. Here, six independently controlled thrust magnitudes form a square wrench map when the six tilt angles are fixed.

Constrained allocation has a substantial history. Active-set methods handle bounded least squares [15], dynamic QPs shape actuator transients [16], and null-space methods enforce hard joint limits [17]. Dual-layer allocation can also modify the requested virtual control when actuator constraints prevent its realization [18]. A recent predictive allocator accounts for asymmetric motor dynamics by optimizing null-space motion over a horizon [19]. Our method instead constrains the servo motion to preserve a specified neighborhood of the desired wrench inside the attainable set.

For the quantitative comparison, we use geometric allocation (GA), augmented differential allocation (ADA), and normalized differential allocation (NDA). Section IV gives their essential equations and the differential-allocation (DA) foundation. Power differential allocation (PDA) additionally uses speed-dependent propeller-acceleration envelopes [10]. A calibrated envelope is unavailable for the present propulsion model, so PDA is excluded from this benchmark.

A differential allocator uses twelve effective actuator coordinates because servo motion and propeller acceleration both contribute to wrench rate. Instantaneous feasibility instead concerns the six thrust channels at fixed angles. A direction available through coordinated motion may therefore be unavailable through thrust changes alone. The proposed barrier constrains this fixed-configuration set while retaining a differential tracking stage.

II-B Barrier Functions and Actuator Feasibility

CBFs translate set invariance into control inequalities [11, 12]. Robust, input-to-state-safe, and measurement-robust formulations address uncertainty in the dynamics, actuation, and state information [20, 21, 22]. Integral and high-order CBFs accommodate dynamically extended inputs and higher-relative-degree constraints [23, 24]. Safety layers have also been studied for aerial physical interaction [25] and reaction-wheel allocation [26].

Readiness barriers preserve a lower bound on motor wrench-rate authority through a torque-level allocation QP [27]. More directly, Silano and Saska [28] use active tilt to preserve a motor-only wrench-rate readiness metric, enforced through motor torques and servo setpoints. Their certificate concerns a lower bound on the log-volume of an attainable wrench-rate approximation. Our constraint follows a specified wrench request: the request and its uncertainty neighborhood must fit inside the instantaneous thrust-limited wrench set. The square inverse map makes this containment test exact, and the equivalent-wrench identity transfers nominal margins to actual-angle feasibility. The distinction is the certified quantity: a desired-wrench neighborhood in the thrust-limited set, rather than a volume measure of motor wrench-rate authority.

The certificate is continuous time and conditional on admissible CBF inputs. Sampled-data and delayed-input formulations [29, 30] address implementation effects, while command governors and predictive safety filters [31, 32] can modify a request that exceeds the available authority. These are complementary extensions to the allocation-level result established here.

The present certificate concerns allocation feasibility; outer-loop stability and task-level safety remain separate properties.

The external force dFd_{F} is expressed in inertial coordinates and the external moment dτd_{\tau} in body coordinates. di​(αi)\displaystyle d_{i}(\alpha_{i}) =cos⁡αi​e3+sin⁡αi​ti,\displaystyle=\cos\alpha_{i}\,e_{3}+\sin\alpha_{i}\,t_{i}, (3)
ai​(αi)\displaystyle a_{i}(\alpha_{i}) =[di​(αi)ri×di​(αi)+si​κi​di​(αi)],\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}d_{i}(\alpha_{i})\\ r_{i}\times d_{i}(\alpha_{i})+s_{i}\kappa_{i}d_{i}(\alpha_{i})\end{bmatrix}, (4)

The vectors α,f∈ℝ6\alpha,f\in\mathbb{R}^{6} contain tilt angles and thrust magnitudes. Propeller speed ωi\omega_{i} is related to thrust by fi=kT,i​ωi2f_{i}=k_{T,i}\omega_{i}^{2} for a positive thrust coefficient kT,ik_{T,i}. Identical co-tilting propellers with the same unit-thrust wrench column can be grouped into one channel by summing their thrusts and bounds. For a pair driven by a common speed command, kT,ik_{T,i} includes both propellers. This reduction preserves the instantaneous attainable wrench set.

The allocator uses body-frame wrenches. Inertial force requests must therefore be rotated before applying (5), and their derivatives must include the rotating-frame term given in Appendix A.

III-B Instantaneous Wrench Feasibility

For constant thrust bounds 0≤f¯<f¯0\leq\underline{f}<\overline{f}, define

𝒰f\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{f} ={f:f¯≤f≤f¯},\displaystyle=\{f:\underline{f}\leq f\leq\overline{f}\}, 𝒲⁡(α)\displaystyle\mathcal{W}(\alpha) =A⁡(α)​𝒰f.\displaystyle=A(\alpha)\mathcal{U}_{f}. (6)

On an open configuration domain D⊂ℝ6D\subset\mathbb{R}^{6} where A⁡(α)A(\alpha) is nonsingular, let C⁡(α)=A​(α)−1C(\alpha)=A(\alpha)^{-1}. Then

wd∈𝒲⁡(α)⟺f¯≤C⁡(α)​wd≤f¯.w_{d}\in\mathcal{W}(\alpha)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \underline{f}\leq C(\alpha)w_{d}\leq\overline{f}. (7)

Although the reduced allocation model has twelve actuator coordinates, only the six channel thrusts remain free at fixed angles. Equation (7) applies only where this square map remains nonsingular; all-vertical rotor directions, for example, cannot provide arbitrary six-dimensional instantaneous wrench.

On DD, the thrust box maps to a full-dimensional parallelotope with twelve facets, each represented by a row of C⁡(α)C(\alpha) and a thrust bound. The inverse-map test gives every feasibility inequality without sampling wrench directions or constructing vertices. This exact reduction relies on the square nonsingular map; a redundant fixed-configuration map requires a different treatment of internal thrust freedom.

III-C Nominal and Actual Servo Configurations

Let αn\alpha_{n} be the nominal servo trajectory and αr\alpha_{r} the actual configuration. Their difference is evaluated in consistently unwrapped angular coordinates. The proposed allocator chooses

α˙n=ν,ν∈𝒱,\dot{\alpha}_{n}=\nu,\qquad\nu\in\mathcal{V}, (8)

where 𝒱={ν:ν¯≤ν≤ν¯}\mathcal{V}=\{\nu:\underline{\nu}\leq\nu\leq\overline{\nu}\} is the admissible nominal servo-rate set. Servo lag permits αr≠αn\alpha_{r}\neq\alpha_{n} and α˙r≠ν\dot{\alpha}_{r}\neq\nu. Our objective is

wd​(t)∈𝒲⁡(αr​(t)).w_{d}(t)\in\mathcal{W}(\alpha_{r}(t)). (9)

This requires a bounded thrust solution at the actual angles. It does not assume that the actual thrust frf_{r} instantaneously equals that solution.

We distinguish the nominal required thrust fn=C⁡(αn)​wdf_{n}=C(\alpha_{n})w_{d}, the actual-configuration requirement C⁡(αr)​wdC(\alpha_{r})w_{d}, the generated thrust frf_{r}, and the command fcf_{c}. They enter the barrier, feasibility test, tracking feedback, and command integrator, respectively.

IV From Geometric to Differential Allocation

We express the baseline methods in the notation of Section III, distinguishing actuator endpoint selection, differential tracking, and rate-limit enforcement. Table I summarizes their roles and the additional containment objective addressed by the proposed CBF-based control allocation (CA) method.

The CBF stage below adds instantaneous wrench-set constraints to rate-based tracking.

V CBF-Based Wrench-Feasibility Allocation

The proposed allocator separates two functions (Fig. 1): the servo stage preserves wrench feasibility, and the thrust stage tracks the requested wrench. We construct a sufficient nominal containment condition for actual-angle feasibility, reduce it exactly to twelve thrust margins, and derive affine constraints on the servo rate.

V-A Robust Allocation Objective

The physical objective is wd∈𝒲⁡(αr)w_{d}\in\mathcal{W}(\alpha_{r}), whereas the servo decision acts on the nominal trajectory α˙n=ν\dot{\alpha}_{n}=\nu. To connect these two configurations, let An=A⁡(αn)A_{n}=A(\alpha_{n}), Ar=A⁡(αr)A_{r}=A(\alpha_{r}), Cn=An−1C_{n}=A_{n}^{-1}, and Cr=Ar−1C_{r}=A_{r}^{-1}. Define the equivalent wrench perturbation induced by configuration mismatch

δ​ws=(An−Ar)​Cr​wd.\delta w_{s}=(A_{n}-A_{r})C_{r}w_{d}. (19)

It gives the exact nominal-to-actual relation

Cr​wd=Cn​(wd+δ​ws).C_{r}w_{d}=C_{n}(w_{d}+\delta w_{s}). (20)

The same vector Cr​wdC_{r}w_{d} produces wdw_{d} through ArA_{r} and wd+δ​wsw_{d}+\delta w_{s} through AnA_{n}. Equation (20) compares the two configurations without linearizing their angle mismatch or equating their servo velocities.

Choose a fixed ellipsoid that bounds this equivalent error over the operating domain:

ℰw={δ:δ⊤​Qw−1​δ≤1},Qw≻0.\mathcal{E}_{w}=\{\delta:\delta^{\top}Q_{w}^{-1}\delta\leq 1\},\qquad Q_{w}\succ 0. (21)

For example, Qw=diag⁡(rF2​I3,rτ2​I3)Q_{w}=\operatorname{diag}(r_{F}^{2}I_{3},r_{\tau}^{2}I_{3}) sets separate force and torque radii. The robust nominal objective is

wd​(t)+ℰw⊆𝒲⁡(αn​(t)).\boxed{\quad w_{d}(t)+\mathcal{E}_{w}\subseteq\mathcal{W}(\alpha_{n}(t)).\quad} (22)

With δ​ws∈ℰw\delta w_{s}\in\mathcal{E}_{w}, this containment makes Cr​wdC_{r}w_{d} an admissible thrust vector by (20). The servo stage must maintain (22) as wdw_{d} changes, subject to the nominal rate limits.

The perturbation δ​ws\delta w_{s} captures configuration mismatch. The tracking error wd−Ar​frw_{d}-A_{r}f_{r} also depends on motor output and supplies feedback to the thrust stage.

V-B Exact Reduction to Thrust Margins

Let ci⊤c_{i}^{\top} denote row ii of CnC_{n}. Define the nominal required thrust and the reserve projected onto thrust channel ii as

fn=Cn​wd,ρi=ci⊤​Qw​ci.f_{n}=C_{n}w_{d},\qquad\rho_{i}=\sqrt{c_{i}^{\top}Q_{w}c_{i}}. (23)

Writing δ=Qw1/2​z\delta=Q_{w}^{1/2}z with ‖z‖2≤1\left\|z\right\|_{2}\leq 1 yields

Bi±≥0∀i⟺wd+ℰw⊆𝒲(αn).B_{i}^{\pm}\geq 0\quad\forall i\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_{d}+\mathcal{E}_{w}\subseteq\mathcal{W}(\alpha_{n}). (27)

Each inequality bounds every point of the same ellipsoid. The worst-case perturbation may differ between channels; the support extrema need not be attained simultaneously.

V-C Analytical Margin Dynamics

Although containment depends nonlinearly on the servo angles, its margin derivatives are affine in the servo rate. From Cn​An=IC_{n}A_{n}=I,

∂Cn∂αn,j=−Cn​∂An∂αn,j​Cn.\frac{\partial C_{n}}{\partial\alpha_{n,j}}=-C_{n}\frac{\partial A_{n}}{\partial\alpha_{n,j}}C_{n}. (28)

Since only column jj of AnA_{n} depends on αn,j\alpha_{n,j}, its derivative follows directly from aj′a_{j}^{\prime}. Define M,P∈ℝ6×6M,P\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times 6} and b∈ℝ6b\in\mathbb{R}^{6} at (αn,wd)(\alpha_{n},w_{d}) by

J¯α\displaystyle\bar{J}_{\alpha} =[a1′(αn,1)fn,1⋯a6′(αn,6)fn,6],\displaystyle=[a_{1}^{\prime}(\alpha_{n,1})f_{n,1}\ \cdots\ a_{6}^{\prime}(\alpha_{n,6})f_{n,6}],
M\displaystyle M =−Cn​J¯α,b=Cn​w˙d,\displaystyle=-C_{n}\bar{J}_{\alpha},\qquad b=C_{n}\dot{w}_{d}, (29)
Pi​j\displaystyle P_{ij} =ci⊤​Qwρi​∂ci∂αn,j.\displaystyle=\frac{c_{i}^{\top}Q_{w}}{\rho_{i}}\frac{\partial c_{i}}{\partial\alpha_{n,j}}. (30)

Differentiating (23) then gives

f˙n\displaystyle\dot{f}_{n} =−Cn​A˙n​fn+Cn​w˙d=M​ν+b,\displaystyle=-C_{n}\dot{A}_{n}f_{n}+C_{n}\dot{w}_{d}=M\nu+b,
ρ˙i\displaystyle\dot{\rho}_{i} =ci⊤​Qw​c˙iρi=(P​ν)i.\displaystyle=\frac{c_{i}^{\top}Q_{w}\dot{c}_{i}}{\rho_{i}}=(P\nu)_{i}. (31)

Stacking the six lower and upper margins as B−B^{-} and B+B^{+} gives

B˙−=(M−P)​ν+b,B˙+=(−M−P)​ν−b.\dot{B}^{-}=(M-P)\nu+b,\qquad\dot{B}^{+}=(-M-P)\nu-b. (32)

These margin dynamics are exact; no finite-angle linearization is used.

A useful closed form makes the geometry dependence explicit. Define Dα=[a1′⋯a6′]D_{\alpha}=[a_{1}^{\prime}\ \cdots\ a_{6}^{\prime}] at αn\alpha_{n} and G=Cn​DαG=C_{n}D_{\alpha}. Equation (28) implies ∂ci/∂αn,j=−Gi​j​cj\partial c_{i}/\partial\alpha_{n,j}=-G_{ij}c_{j}, and hence

Mi​j=−Gi​j​fn,j,Pi​j=−Gi​j​ci⊤​Qw​cjρi.M_{ij}=-G_{ij}f_{n,j},\qquad P_{ij}=-G_{ij}\frac{c_{i}^{\top}Q_{w}c_{j}}{\rho_{i}}. (33)

The coefficient Gi​jG_{ij} couples servo jj to both required thrust and reserve in channel ii. A motion can reduce fn,if_{n,i} while increasing ρi\rho_{i}, so differentiating required thrust alone is insufficient.

The term b=Cn​w˙db=C_{n}\dot{w}_{d} accounts for motion of the requested wrench. Substituting vwv_{w} for w˙d\dot{w}_{d} would omit this motion when w=wdw=w_{d}, because the feedback target then vanishes. Appendix A derives w˙d\dot{w}_{d} for representative translational and attitude controllers, including frame rotation and compensation terms.

V-D Servo-Rate Quadratic Program

With the linear extended class-𝒦\mathcal{K} choice γ​Bi±\gamma B_{i}^{\pm}, γ>0\gamma>0, the required barrier inequalities are

B˙i±+γBi±≥0,i=1,…,6.\dot{B}_{i}^{\pm}+\gamma B_{i}^{\pm}\geq 0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,6. (34)

These inequalities yield the complete servo QP:

ν∗=arg⁡minν∈ℝ612​ν⊤​Rν​ν+12​‖M​ν+b‖Rf2subject to(M−P)​ν+b+γ​B−≥0,(−M−P)​ν−b+γ​B+≥0,ν¯≤ν≤ν¯.\boxed{\begin{aligned} \nu^{*}=\underset{\nu\in\mathbb{R}^{6}}{\arg\min}\quad&\tfrac{1}{2}\nu^{\top}R_{\nu}\nu+\tfrac{1}{2}\left\|M\nu+b\right\|_{R_{f}}^{2}\\[2.0pt] \text{subject to}\quad&(M-P)\nu+b+\gamma B^{-}\geq 0,\\ &(-M-P)\nu-b+\gamma B^{+}\geq 0,\\ &\underline{\nu}\leq\nu\leq\overline{\nu}.\end{aligned}} (35)

Here Rν≻0R_{\nu}\succ 0, Rf⪰0R_{f}\succeq 0, and ‖x‖Rf2=x⊤​Rf​x\left\|x\right\|_{R_{f}}^{2}=x^{\top}R_{f}x. All vector inequalities are componentwise. The twelve barrier constraints preserve the tightened thrust intervals; the rate box bounds α˙n\dot{\alpha}_{n}, not the actual rate α˙r\dot{\alpha}_{r}. The nominal command is obtained by integrating α˙n=ν∗\dot{\alpha}_{n}=\nu^{*}. This trajectory is retained as the state of the certificate; replacing it by the measured angle at each update defines different barrier dynamics.

In (35), bb, M​νM\nu, and P​νP\nu represent requested-wrench motion, reorientation, and reserve variation, respectively.

The cost penalizes servo motion and nominal required-thrust rate. The latter regularizes reconfiguration without imposing a hard motor-acceleration limit. The Hessian H=Rν+M⊤​Rf​M≻0H=R_{\nu}+M^{\top}R_{f}M\succ 0 gives a unique minimizer whenever the feasible set is nonempty. With Rf=0R_{f}=0, the QP selects the feasible servo rate with minimum RνR_{\nu}-weighted norm and leaves the servos stationary when zero rate is admissible.

V-E Boundary Behavior

The two barrier inequalities for channel ii can be written as a single interval for the nominal required-thrust rate:

ρ˙i−γ​Bi−≤f˙n,i≤−ρ˙i+γ​Bi+.\dot{\rho}_{i}-\gamma B_{i}^{-}\ \leq\ \dot{f}_{n,i}\ \leq\ -\dot{\rho}_{i}+\gamma B_{i}^{+}. (36)

At the lower boundary, Bi−=0B_{i}^{-}=0 requires f˙n,i≥ρ˙i\dot{f}_{n,i}\geq\dot{\rho}_{i}: required thrust must keep pace with a growing reserve. At the upper boundary, Bi+=0B_{i}^{+}=0 requires f˙n,i≤−ρ˙i\dot{f}_{n,i}\leq-\dot{\rho}_{i}: required thrust must decrease as the reserve grows. Holding fn,if_{n,i} constant is insufficient when reconfiguration consumes additional reserve.

Positive margins relax the interval endpoints by γ​Bi±\gamma B_{i}^{\pm}. Larger γ\gamma permits faster approach to a boundary, while QwQ_{w} sets the reserved authority. Changing γ\gamma neither enlarges the thrust box nor changes uncertainty coverage. At the boundary, the inward-pointing derivative condition is independent of γ\gamma.

A common ν∈𝒱\nu\in\mathcal{V} must satisfy all six intervals; separate interval feasibility is insufficient. The QP enforces these coupled inequalities jointly. For constant wdw_{d}, nonnegative margins, and a rate box containing zero, ν=0\nu=0 is feasible and minimizes the cost. The nominal geometry can remain fixed while motor feedback addresses wrench-tracking error.

subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} u¯f,k≤uf≤u¯f,k.\displaystyle\underline{u}_{f,k}\leq u_{f}\leq\overline{u}_{f,k}.

Here kk indexes command updates, Δ​t>0\Delta t>0 is their period, and the maximum and minimum act componentwise. For fc,0∈𝒰ff_{c,0}\in\mathcal{U}_{f} and u¯f≤0≤u¯f\underline{u}_{f}\leq 0\leq\overline{u}_{f}, zero rate remains admissible and (39) keeps fcf_{c} inside 𝒰f\mathcal{U}_{f}.

Without active bounds or regularization, the solution reduces to uf=Cr​(vw−Jα​α˙^r)u_{f}=C_{r}(v_{w}-J_{\alpha}\widehat{\dot{\alpha}}_{r}). The objective uses a command-rate approximation; motor dynamics determine how frf_{r} follows fcf_{c}, so uf=f˙ru_{f}=\dot{f}_{r} is not an assumed physical identity. The measured or estimated servo-rate term accounts for wrench change already caused by reorientation. Thus, thrust tracking uses actual actuator feedback, while the nominal trajectory defines the robust certificate proved next.

VI Wrench-Feasibility Guarantee

VI-A Conditional Forward Invariance

The certificate set is 𝒞={(αn,wd)∈D×ℝ6:B−≥0,B+≥0}\mathcal{C}=\{(\alpha_{n},w_{d})\in D\times\mathbb{R}^{6}:B^{-}\geq 0,\ B^{+}\geq 0\}. Let αn\alpha_{n}, αr\alpha_{r}, and wdw_{d} be locally absolutely continuous on I=[t0,T)I=[t_{0},T), with both angle trajectories in DD and α˙n=ν\dot{\alpha}_{n}=\nu almost everywhere. Assume A∈C1​(D,ℝ6×6)A\in C^{1}(D;\mathbb{R}^{6\times 6}) is nonsingular.

Theorem 1

Suppose (i) Bi±​(t0)≥0B_{i}^{\pm}(t_{0})\geq 0 for all ii; (ii) δ​ws​(t)∈ℰw\delta w_{s}(t)\in\mathcal{E}_{w} on II; and (iii) the selected locally integrable command satisfies the hard constraints of (35) almost everywhere, using the total derivative w˙d\dot{w}_{d}. Then

Bi±​(t)\displaystyle B_{i}^{\pm}(t) ≥e−γ⁡(t−t0)​Bi±​(t0)≥0,\displaystyle\geq e^{-\gamma(t-t_{0})}B_{i}^{\pm}(t_{0})\geq 0, (40)
f¯+B−​(t)\displaystyle\underline{f}+B^{-}(t) ≤Cr​(t)​wd​(t)≤f¯−B+​(t).\displaystyle\leq C_{r}(t)w_{d}(t)\leq\overline{f}-B^{+}(t). (41)

For all t∈It\in I, (αn,wd)(\alpha_{n},w_{d}) remains in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and each required-thrust margin at the actual angles is at least its corresponding nominal barrier margin.

Proof:

The stated regularity and Qw≻0Q_{w}\succ 0 make the margins locally absolutely continuous. Equations (35) and (32) imply B˙i±+γ​Bi±≥0\dot{B}_{i}^{\pm}+\gamma B_{i}^{\pm}\geq 0 almost everywhere. Multiplication by eγ⁡(t−t0)e^{\gamma(t-t_{0})} and integration yield (40).

Since δ​ws∈ℰw\delta w_{s}\in\mathcal{E}_{w}, the ellipsoid support gives |ci⊤​δ​ws|≤ρi|c_{i}^{\top}\delta w_{s}|\leq\rho_{i}. By (20), the actual required thrust satisfies

fn,i−ρi≤(Cr​wd)i≤fn,i+ρi.f_{n,i}-\rho_{i}\leq(C_{r}w_{d})_{i}\leq f_{n,i}+\rho_{i}. (42)

Substituting fn,i−ρi=f¯i+Bi−f_{n,i}-\rho_{i}=\underline{f}_{i}+B_{i}^{-} and fn,i+ρi=f¯i−Bi+f_{n,i}+\rho_{i}=\overline{f}_{i}-B_{i}^{+} gives (41). Nonnegative margins therefore ensure actual-configuration feasibility. ∎Bounded mismatch thus transfers nominal containment to the actual configuration without equating nominal and actual servo rates. The guarantee holds along an admissible solution of (35); recursive QP feasibility and instantaneous thrust realization are not conclusions of the theorem.

VII Simulation Study

VII-A Setup and Scenarios

The study uses an actively tilting vehicle with six servo joints and twelve propellers in MuJoCo [33]. Each pair of propellers shares a tilt angle and an identical unit-thrust wrench column, so its two thrusts form one effective channel in (5). The recorded per-propeller command range is 00–88 N, giving 0≤fi≤160\leq f_{i}\leq 16 N for each pair. The setup includes servo and thrust dynamics and a PID outer controller with a nonlinear robust internal-loop compensator (NRIC) [34]. The explicitly recorded outer-controller settings are common to all four methods and are summarized in Table III.

Results labeled Proposed CBF-based CA use the measured-angle prototype of the proposed allocator. The formulation in Sections V–VI additionally requires a persistent nominal trajectory and an explicit configuration-mismatch reserve. Accordingly, this study evaluates tracking and actual-angle wrench feasibility; direct validation of the nominal-trajectory certificate requires further records.

Table II defines the four scenarios, and Fig. 3 shows their representative scenes. For the cartwheel, the command specifies a 2 s takeoff, 1 s hold, 2 s pitch transition, and 1 s post-pitch hold. Continuous body yaw begins at t=6t=6 s. Servo position limits are disabled for this continuous rotation. The circular reference has speed 3.143.14 m/s and acceleration 6.586.58 m/s2 on its constant-speed segment. Each run contains 20 s of telemetry at 8 ms intervals; this is the logging interval, not the controller period. The preserved records support reproducible telemetry analysis but lack complete allocator gains, null-space targets, and actuator-model settings for a full simulation rerun.

Both maneuvers vary the body-frame wrench demand. The 1 Hz external forces in S2 and S4 act through the vehicle dynamics and feedback command; they do not define the configuration-mismatch ellipsoid in (21).
